case.text: Extracted KOI889 observing note from ExoFOP-Kepler on 2020-11-02 The following paper that discusses the measurement of the mass of this KOI has been posted to the archive. Title: "KOI-200b and KOI-889b: two transiting exoplanets detected and characterized with Kepler, SOPHIE and HARPS-N" Abstract: "We present the detection and characterization of the two new transiting, close-in, giant extrasolar planets KOI-200b and KOI-889b. They were first identified by the Kepler team as promising candidates from photometry of the Kepler satellite, then we established their planetary nature thanks to the radial velocity follow-up jointly secured with the spectrographs SOPHIE and HARPS-N. Combined analyses of the whole datasets allow the two planetary systems to be characterized. The planet KOI-200b has mass and radius of 0.68 +/- 0.09 M_Jup and 1.32 +/- 0.14 R_Jup; it orbits in 7.34 days a F8V host star with mass and radius of 1.40 (+0.14/-0.11) M_Sun and 1.51 +/- 0.14 R_Sun. KOI-889b is a massive planet with mass and radius of 9.9 +/- 0.5 M_Jup and 1.03 +/- 0.06 R_Jup; it orbits in 8.88 days an active G8V star with a rotation period of 19.2 +/- 0.3 days, and mass and radius of 0.88 +/- 0.06 M_Sun and 0.88 +/- 0.04 R_Sun. Both planets lie on eccentric orbits and are located just at the frontier between regimes where the tides can explain circularization and where tidal effects are negligible. The two planets are among the first ones detected and characterized thanks to observations secured with HARPS-N, the new spectrograph recently mounted at the Telescopio Nazionale Galileo. These results illustrate the benefits that could be obtained from joint studies using two spectrographs as SOPHIE and HARPS-N. " link: http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013arXiv1304.6002H Extracted KOI889 observing note from ExoFOP-Kepler on 2020-11-02 Robo-AO LP600-imaging of KOI-889 on 2014-07-16 No companions detected within 4.0" https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.03584

This test has the great value of detecting any companion star, especially G or K-type stars, that might be blended with the primary star. I attach a representative set of these cross-correlation functions (actually chi^2). The narrow dip is the chi^2 statistic of the spectrum of KOI-20 with the solar spectrum, as a function of displacement of the two in units of km/s. The line width is ~5 km/s, consistent with the low rotational Vsini of 1 km/s for the star. Any companion star 10% the brightness of the primary star (KOI-20) would easily show up as a second dip, which is not seen. Thus we can rule out any companions that are brighter than 10% that of the star. For gravitationally bound companions, this rules out any other G-type stars and the K0 stars, i.e. 0.8 - 1.0 Msun. The only way such a star could hide would be if it had the same line-of-sight velocity as the primary star, and also didn't change velocity during the year, which seem unlikely if it had a tertiary star ("C") that causing the dimmings. Therefore, the absence of a second dip in the cross correlation (chi^2) rules out G-type companions. And it rules out all background stars within 1 arcsec having a brightness greater than 10% that of the primary.
